t: Converting colors to CMYK or RGB
h: Converting the colors What is converted How the colors are worked out
x: Converting colors to CMYK or RGB A drawing often mixes colors defined in RGB (for screens) with colors defined in CMYK (for printing inks). Before you send a drawing to print, or reuse a print job on the web, Tools > Convert Colors turns every color of the selected objects, or of the whole drawing, into one model in a single step. Converting the colors To convert only some objects, select them first. Choose Tools > Convert Colors. Under Convert to, choose CMYK (the default) or RGB. Under Colors of, choose The selected objects (the default when something is selected) or The whole drawing, which also takes in the pages' backgrounds and the symbols. Tick Convert spot colors too to turn spot colors into their CMYK or RGB mix as well (off at first). Click OK. The status bar says how many colors changed. All the changes undo in one step. When every color is already in the model you chose, or nothing is selected, nothing changes. What is converted Solid fills, the stops of gradients, the colors of mesh fills, patterns and textures. Outlines, text and table cells. The colors of effects (contours, blends, extrusions, bevels, block shadows and the others) and of drop shadows. Objects inside groups and clip frames, at any depth. Bitmaps take the color mode: converted to CMYK, a picture's pixels change to show the colors the inks can print; converted to RGB, only the mode changes and the pixels stay. See Bitmap color modes. The registration color never changes, so marks still print on every plate. Spot colors stay spot colors unless you tick Convert spot colors too. A color that is already in the model stays as it is. How the colors are worked out The conversion goes through the color management profiles: the drawing's own CMYK profile when it carries one, else the RGB and CMYK profiles, the rendering intent and the black point setting of Tools > Color Management. See Color management. Tip: A color converted to CMYK and back to RGB is not the color you started with when it was too bright for the inks. Keep a copy of the drawing before converting a whole drawing.

Speciale effecten Effecten veranderen hoe een object eruitziet zonder het object zelf te veranderen: een overvloeiing vult de ruimte tussen twee objecten, een contour tekent ringen om een object, een envelop buigt het, een extrusie laat het massief lijken, een schaduw tilt het van de pagina. De meeste effecten zijn dynamisch: het object houdt zijn eigen vorm, en het effect wordt ervan afgeleid, zodat u het effect altijd kunt wijzigen of verwijderen. De effecten staan in het menu Effecten, in het uitklapmenu Effecten van de gereedschapskist en in eigen panelen. Bitmapeffecten veranderen de pixels van afbeeldingen, of van objecten die als afbeelding worden getekend.

h: Managing effects Other effect commands
x: The Effects panel An object can carry several live effects at once, applied one after the other. The Effects panel lists the effects of the selected object in the order they apply, from the top down. Open it with Window > Panels > Effects.  Managing effects Each row of the list has: a check box that turns the effect on or off. An effect turned off keeps its place and settings, but is not drawn, exported or printed; the effect's name, dimmed while it is off; up and down arrows that move the effect earlier or later, which changes the result (for example a contour of an envelope, or an envelope of a contour); a cross that removes the effect. Every change is one undo step. Each effect is still edited with its own tool or panel. Other effect commands Effects > Flatten Effects turns the effects of the selected objects into plain objects. Effect Picker shows a list of effects to apply to the selection. Object > Clear Effect removes the effect of the selection. Object > Copy Effect copies an effect from another object, and Clone Effect makes a clone that follows it; see Copying and cloning effects.

h: To blend two objects Blend settings Controls on the canvas Blending along a path Removing or splitting a blend Saving as .cdr
x: Blends A blend draws a series of intermediate steps between two objects, changing shape, size and color from one to the other. Use it for smooth shading, repeated patterns or a shape that turns into another. To blend two objects With the tool: Choose the Blend tool from the Effects flyout. Drag from the start object to the end object. With the panel: Select two objects. Open the Blend panel with Effects > Blend (Ctrl+F8). Set the options and click Apply.  Both objects stay objects of the drawing: move, resize or recolor either one and the steps follow. Deleting the end object removes the blend. Blend settings With a blend selected, every change on the property bar or in the panel applies at once. Blend steps: the number of steps (5 at first, up to 999). Spacing, for a blend on a path: the distance between steps; the number of steps follows from the length of the path. Rotation: turns the steps progressively; Loop turns them about the middle between the two objects instead. Acceleration: the object slider makes the steps crowd towards one end; the color slider does the same for the colors. Apply to sizing makes the object acceleration change the sizes too, and Link acceleration keeps the two sliders together. Reset puts both back to even. Color Blend: Direct (straight from one color to the other), Clockwise or Counterclockwise (around the color wheel). The tool's property bar has the steps, rotation and the two accelerations. Controls on the canvas Pick a blend with the Blend tool (click its start or end object, or a step) to show its controls: a square on the start object, a crossed square on the end object, the line between them and two sliders on it, the object acceleration above and the color acceleration below. Drag a slider toward the start or the end to crowd the steps or the colors there. The blend follows live, each drag is one undo step, and the property bar follows. A slider goes as far one way as the other: at 100 % the middle step sits right by the start object, at -100 % right by the end object. Drag an end square to move its object, so the blend changes direction. Drop it on another object to make that object the new start or end, with the blend's settings. The object acceleration moves the steps toward one end also when the blend follows no path. A bitmap effect on the start object keeps the blend drawn. Blending along a path Select the blend. Click New path in the Blend panel and click a curve. The steps follow the curve. Rotate all objects turns each step along the curve, and Blend along full path places the first and last steps at the ends of the curve. Removing or splitting a blend Clear blend removes the steps and leaves both objects. Break apart turns the steps into objects of their own, grouped. Object > Break Blend Group Apart (Ctrl+K, also on the right-click menu) does the same. Saving as .cdr A blend saved as .cdr (version 9 or later) stays a blend: the file holds the two objects and the blend record between them, so the program that opens the file shows the steps and lets you change the blend. The steps, spacing and the two objects go into the file; acceleration, rotation, a path and the colour direction come back in TraceDraw (version 14 or later), other programs start from their defaults.

h: To add a contour Contour settings
x: Contours A contour draws evenly spaced copies of an object's outline inside it, outside it, or to its center, like the lines of a map. It is a live effect: change the object and the contour follows. To add a contour With the tool: Choose the Contour tool from the Effects flyout. Drag from an object: away from its middle for an outside contour, towards it for an inside one. The further you drag, the larger the spacing. With the panel: Select an object. Open the Contour panel with Effects > Contour (Ctrl+F9). Set the options and click Apply.  Groups and bitmaps cannot take a contour. Contour settings The property bar and the panel show the settings of the selected contour and change it at once. To center, Inside or Outside (at first). Steps: 3 at first, up to 999. To center makes as many as fit. Offset: the distance between steps (2 mm at first). Corners: mitered (sharp, at first), round or beveled. Color direction: direct, clockwise or counterclockwise around the color wheel, from the object's colors to the last step's. The fill and outline colors of the last step (white and black at first). An object without a fill gives unfilled steps. Object acceleration and color acceleration (-100 to 100%) crowd the steps or the colors towards the object or towards the last step. Outside steps are drawn behind the object, inside steps in front of it. Clear contour removes the contour; Break apart turns the steps into objects, grouped beside the object. Object > Break Contour Group Apart (Ctrl+K, also on the right-click menu) does the same.

h: To distort an object Distortion settings
x: Distortion The Distort tool bends an object's outline in three ways: push and pull (spikes or petals), zipper (zigzag teeth) and twister (a swirl). It is a live effect: you can change, move or remove the distortion at any time, and the object keeps its own outline. To distort an object Choose the Distort tool from the Effects flyout. Choose the kind on the property bar. Drag on the object. The distortion is centered where you start. Push and pull: drag right to push the nodes out (spiky shapes with hollow sides), left to pull them in (rounded petals). A straight side bends from its middle, so a square pulled in gets four round lobes. Zipper: the further you drag, the taller the teeth. Twister: drag around the starting point; full turns count. The handle follows the pointer as far out or as near as you drag it and stays that long; its length does not change the twist. The center of a selected distortion shows as a diamond: drag it to move the center. Dragging again replaces the distortion; an object has at most one. Groups and bitmaps are not distorted. Distortion settings The property bar shows and changes the selected distortion: the kind: Push and pull, Zipper or Twister (choosing another kind changes a selected distortion); for push and pull, the amplitude (-200 to 200, 20 at first); for zipper, the amplitude (0 to 100 mm, 2 mm at first) and the frequency (teeth per segment, 6 at first), with Random (uneven teeth), Smooth (rounded teeth) and Local (teeth shrink away from the center); for twister, clockwise or counterclockwise, the number of whole rotations and the extra degrees. A value changed on the property bar shows on the selected object at once, also when it has no distortion yet. The zipper draws one more line than its frequency, and its amplitude, frequency and angle have handles on the page to drag. The twister spirals smoothly to the ends of a shape. Object > Clear Effect removes the distortion.

h: To add an envelope Editing the frame Envelope settings
x: Envelopes An envelope is a frame of nodes around an object; the object is bent to fill the frame, and follows when you move its nodes. Use it to arch text, bulge a shape or fit artwork into a flag or a circle. The object keeps its own shape, so the envelope can be changed or removed at any time. To add an envelope With the tool: Choose the Envelope tool from the Effects flyout. Click an object. It gets a frame of eight nodes: the corners and the middle of each side. Drag the nodes to reshape the frame. With the panel (Effects > Envelope, Ctrl+F7): Select an object. Click Add new, or click one of the 24 preset shapes (arch, circle, flag, heart, cloud, speech bubble and more) to use it as the envelope.  Editing the frame The editing mode, chosen on the property bar or in the panel, decides what happens to the sides when you drag a node: Straight line: the sides stay straight; Single arc: the sides become one smooth arc; Double arc: the sides become S curves; Unconstrained (at first): the node carries its handles; click a node to see its two handles and drag them to bend each side on its own. Double-click the frame to add a node, a node (other than a corner) to delete it. In the unconstrained mode the property bar also has Add node and Delete node. The Shape tool edits the frame the same way. Envelope settings Presets on the property bar: arch, bulge, squeeze, flag, perspective and circle. Mapping, how the object fills the frame: Putty (at first), Original (spread evenly along the frame), Horizontal or Vertical (only across or only up). Keep lines: straight segments of the object stay straight. Add new envelope puts a fresh frame around the object as it now looks, over the envelope it has. Copy envelope properties: click another object to copy its envelope (as Object > Copy Effect > Envelope From). Click an object without an envelope, such as a circle, a star or a curve you drew, to fit the selected text or objects into its shape. Clear envelope removes the last envelope.

h: Place the photo and the design Follow the chest with an envelope Let the cloth show through: Multiply Keep the print on the shirt: a clip frame Tips
x: Making a T-shirt mockup A mockup shows a design on a photo of the real thing, here a T-shirt, so you can judge it before it is printed. Four tools from the rest of this Help do the work: an envelope bends the design over the chest, a transparency merge mode lets the cloth's folds and shading show through the print, and a clip frame keeps the print on the shirt.  Place the photo and the design Choose File > Import and import a photo of a plain shirt, front view, in good light. Draw or import your design, place it over the chest and size it there. If the design is made of several objects, select them all and choose Object > Group, so the next steps treat it as one. Follow the chest with an envelope Cloth is not flat. A slight curve makes the print look as if it lies on the shirt. Select the design and choose the Envelope tool (or open Effects > Envelope). Use Single arc and drag the middle nodes a little: the bottom one down, the top one up and the side ones out. Keep it subtle. Each object of a group is bent from the box of the whole group and keeps its own colours. See Envelopes.  Let the cloth show through: Multiply A print takes on the shading of the cloth under it. The Multiply merge mode does the same: each color is multiplied by what is beneath, so the folds and shadows of the photo darken the design where they darken the shirt. Select the design and choose the Transparency tool, or open the transparency settings in the Properties panel. Choose Uniform and set the amount low (0 to 10 %). Set Merge mode to Multiply. See Transparency.  Keep the print on the shirt: a clip frame A large print, or one placed near a sleeve, can reach past the shirt's edges.  Draw the outline of the shirt over the photo with the Bezier or Pen tool, following its edges (it does not need to be exact where the print does not reach). Give it no fill and no outline. Select the design, choose Object > Clip to Frame > Place Inside Frame and click the outline. The print is cut to the shirt and keeps its Multiply merge mode: it still mixes with the photo beneath the frame. See Placing objects inside a frame.  Tips A white or light shirt shows Multiply best. On a dark shirt, try If Lighter for a light print, or keep Normal with a little transparency. To try another design, use Edit Contents, or Extract Contents, replace the design and place the new one inside again. Group the photo, the frame and the design to move the whole mockup.

h: To extrude an object Extrusion settings
x: Extrusions An extrusion turns a flat object into a solid-looking body, with sides that run from its outline to a copy of it, lit and shaded. It is a live effect: change the object and the body follows. To extrude an object With the tool: Choose the Extrude tool from the Effects flyout. Drag from an object. For a parallel extrusion the body runs along the drag; for the others the end of the drag is the vanishing point. Drag the handle (a square with a cross) to move the vanishing point. With the panel (Effects > Extrude, Ctrl+F10): select an object, set the options and click Apply.  Groups and bitmaps cannot be extruded. Extrusion settings The panel has five pages, chosen with the buttons at its top; the property bar has the main settings and a 3D menu with the rest. Camera: the type of extrusion: small back (at first), big back, small front, big front, back parallel or front parallel. Back types grow behind the object, front types in front of it. The depth (1 to 99, 20 at first), the vanishing point (X and Y, counted from the page origin or the object's center), and whether it is locked to the object (moves with it) or to the page. For parallel types, X and Y are the offset. Rotation: turns the body in space about X, Y and Z (-360 to 360 degrees); Reset puts it back. Lighting: the angle (135 degrees at first), intensity (50 at first) and elevation of the light, and two more lights you can turn on. Color: Object fill (the object's color, at first), Solid (one color) or Shade (a gradient from one color to another on each side). Bevel: a beveled edge on the front face, with its width. Clear extrude removes the extrusion; Break apart turns the faces into objects, grouped beside the object. Object > Break Extrude Group Apart (Ctrl+K, also on the right-click menu) does the same.

h: To add a block shadow Settings
x: Block shadows A block shadow is a solid shadow that runs straight out from an object, as if the object were a thick block. It is drawn below the object as one filled shape, which suits signs and cut vinyl. To add a block shadow Choose the Block Shadow tool from the Effects flyout. Drag from an object in the direction the shadow should go. Settings On the property bar: Depth: how far the shadow reaches. Direction: its angle, 0 being to the right, counterclockwise. Color: 60% black at first. Gap: a clear band between the object and the shadow (0 at first). Clear block shadow removes the effect. With a shadowed object selected, the fields change its shadow; otherwise they set the next one.

h: To add a drop shadow Settings
x: Drop shadows A drop shadow is a soft shadow beneath an object, as if it floated above the page. It is a copy of the object's silhouette in the shadow color, offset and blurred. To add a drop shadow Choose the Drop Shadow tool from the Effects flyout. Drag from an object to where the shadow should fall. Clip frames and groups take shadows too: a frame casts the shadow of what it shows (its fill and the contents within it), and a group the shadow of each of its objects. A click on a shadow with the Pick tool selects its object; with the Drop Shadow tool it shows the shadow's handles, and a drag on the shadow moves it. Shadows show in exported and printed PDF files, with their color, opacity and feathering. Settings On the property bar: the offset of the shadow (2 mm right and 2 mm down at first); its opacity (50% at first); its feathering, how soft its edge is (15% at first); its color (black at first). A change there applies at once to the selected objects, also to an object that has no shadow yet: choose Flat, or an edge, to give it that kind of shadow directly. Shadow handles can be grabbed from a little outside the squares. Object > Clear Effect removes the shadow. To copy the shadow of another object, use Object > Copy Effect > Drop Shadow From.

h: Een object een schuine rand geven
x: Schuine randen Een schuine rand laat de randen van een object verhoogd of uitgesneden lijken, door één kant van de rand te belichten en de andere te beschaduwen. Het is een live-effect, ingesteld in het paneel Schuine rand; open het met Effecten > Schuine rand.  Een object een schuine rand geven Selecteer een gevuld object. Kies in het paneel Schuine rand de stijl: Zachte rand: de rand loopt schuin het object in, aan één kant belicht en aan de andere beschaduwd; Reliëf: het object lijkt uit de pagina gedrukt. Stel het uiterlijk van de schuine rand in: Diepte: hoe ver de schuine rand van de rand af reikt, het object in bij een zachte rand en eruit bij reliëf; Niveau: in hoeveel stappen licht en schaduw over de schuine rand worden verdeeld. 1 geeft twee vlakke tinten, meer stappen laten ze zacht verlopen vanaf de rand naar binnen; Lichthoek: de richting waaruit het licht komt; Intensiteit: hoe sterk licht en schaduw zijn; Lichtkleur en Schaduwkleur: de kleuren van de belichte en de beschaduwde kant; Reliëfkleur: de kleur waaruit de schuine rand wordt getint. Vink het vakje aan en kies een eigen kleur; uitgeschakeld wordt de vulling van het object gebruikt. Klik op Toepassen. Om een schuine rand van een ander object te kopiëren, gebruikt u Object > Effect kopiëren > Schuine rand van. Object > Effect wissen verwijdert haar. Het paneel voor extrusies heeft ook een schuine rand voor het voorvlak; zie Extrusies.

h: To make a lens Kinds of lens Options
x: Lenses A lens changes how the objects beneath it look, without changing them: it can brighten, tint, magnify, invert or apply bitmap effects to everything it covers. Move the lens and the view through it changes. Lenses are set in the Lens panel (Effects > Lens, Alt+F3).  To make a lens Draw a closed object over the objects to change, and select it. In the Lens panel, choose the kind of lens and its settings. Click Apply. Kinds of lens Brighten brightens (or darkens) what lies beneath rate, -100 to 100 (50) Color add adds a color, as light color and rate Color limit lets only a color through color and rate Custom color map maps dark to light onto a range of colors from and to colors, direction Fish eye bulges what lies beneath rate, -1000 to 1000 (100) Heat map shows brightness as warm and cold colors palette rotation Invert inverts the colors  Magnify enlarges what lies beneath amount, 1 to 100 (2) Tinted grayscale shows it in shades of one color color Transparency makes the lens see-through, tinted rate and color Wireframe shows the objects as outlines outline and fill colors Bitmap effects runs bitmap effects over what lies beneath Add effect, in order Options Frozen: keeps what the lens shows now, even when the objects beneath change. Viewpoint: shows another place through the lens. Remove face: shows the lens only over other objects, not over the empty page. To add a bitmap effect as a lens from the effect picker, choose Effects > Effect Picker and apply it as a lens.

h: Adding perspective to an object Drawing in perspective
x: Perspective Perspective makes an object look as if it lay on a plane that recedes into the distance. You can add perspective to an object you have drawn, or draw straight onto a perspective grid. Adding perspective to an object Select an object. Choose Object > Add Perspective. Drag the four corner nodes with the Shape tool to tilt it. To copy the perspective of another object, use Object > Copy Effect > Perspective From. Drawing in perspective View > Draw in Perspective shows a perspective grid over the page. While it is on, every object a drawing tool makes (rectangles, ellipses, polygons, curves, brush strokes, text frames) is laid onto the active plane of the grid. Objects you paste, duplicate or move with the Pick tool stay as they are. The bar at the top left of the drawing window has: Finish: leaves the mode; the objects keep their perspective; 1-Point, 2-Point and 3-Point: the kind of grid; the planes: Ground, Left, Right (and Top for a 1-point grid). The active plane is drawn strongly; Grid: shows the grid lines; Depth (5 to 98%): how far the grid reaches towards the vanishing points; Put on plane: lays the selected objects onto the active plane. Drag the vanishing points (circles) and the near corners (squares) to change the grid. An object laid on a plane gets an ordinary perspective effect, whose four corners you can still edit with the Shape tool.

h: Copying an effect Cloning an effect
x: Copying and cloning effects Instead of setting up an effect again, you can copy it from an object that already has it. Copying an effect Select the objects that should get the effect. Choose Object > Copy Effect and the kind of effect: Drop Shadow From, Transparency From, Envelope From, Perspective From, Distortion From, Extrude From, Contour From, Blend From, Lens From, Bevel From or Block Shadow From. Click the object to copy from. A right-click cancels. The effect is fitted to each object: an envelope or perspective is stretched to its size, a distortion keeps its center at the same place within it. When the object you click has no such effect, nothing changes and the status bar says so. The copy is one undo step. Cloning an effect Object > Clone Effect copies the shadow (Shadow From) or the transparency (Transparency From) of another object, and keeps following it: change the source and the clones change too, until you edit a clone's own effect. Edit > Clone makes a clone of a whole object, and Copy Properties From (Ctrl+Shift+A) copies the fill, outline or text properties of another object: tick what to copy (outline pen, outline color, fill, text properties), click OK, then click the object to copy from.

h: Vector Mosaic Picture Mosaic
x: Vector and picture mosaics A mosaic rebuilds the selected objects, or a picture, out of many small tiles. A vector mosaic uses colored shapes; a picture mosaic uses photos from a folder of your own. Vector Mosaic Open the Vector Mosaic panel with Effects > Vector Mosaic.  Select the objects or bitmaps to turn into a mosaic. Set the options: Density: tiles per inch (10 at first); Scale: the size of each tile within its cell (1 at first); Screen angle: how the rows are turned (30 degrees at first). Keep original: off deletes the selection once the mosaic is made. Limit colors: reduce the tiles to at most that many colors (16 at first). Method: Uniform (every tile full size, transparency flattened on white), Size modulation 1 (the tile size follows the opacity, at first) or Size modulation 2 (darker areas give bigger tiles). Merge adjacent: combine up to that many neighbouring tiles of one color; Weld adjacent overlap: one curve per color instead of one object per tile. Shape: circle (at first), square or custom. For a custom tile, select a closed curve and click Select. Click Apply. The mosaic is one group placed on top of the selection, and is selected. Picture Mosaic Open the Picture Mosaic panel with Effects > Picture Mosaic.  Select the objects or bitmaps to rebuild. Under Library, click Browse and choose a folder of pictures (PNG, JPEG, BMP, GIF, WebP or TIFF; up to 1000). The panel shows how many it holds. Set the options: Keep original (on at first). Columns: tiles across (30 at first); the rows follow from the shape of the selection. Blending: how much of the selection shows over the tiles (20% at first). Allow duplicates (on), with the tile spacing: the fewest tiles between two uses of one picture. Composition: single, stack or array; Edges: stretch the last row or remove it; Output priority and the resolution: how large the mosaic is in pixels. The panel shows the resulting size. Click Apply. Note: Picture libraries need the desktop version; the browser version cannot read folders.

h: To apply a bitmap effect The effect groups Special dialogs Editing the effects of an object The Effect Picker Effects that spread past the edges
x: Bitmap effects Bitmap effects change pixels: blur, sharpen, adjust colors, add textures and artistic strokes. They work on bitmaps and also on vector objects, which are then drawn as the picture the effects make while keeping their own shape, fill and outline. Effects are kept apart from the original pixels: you can edit, hide, reorder or remove any of them later, and removing the last one gives the original back. To apply a bitmap effect Select one or more objects. Choose a group in the Effects menu and an effect. Effects without settings apply at once. The others open a dialog box you can size, with the first selected object before and after in the Before and After preview and the settings on the right. The effect also shows on the drawing and follows every value as it changes (untick Preview to switch that off); the work is done in the background, so the window keeps answering on large pictures. Click OK to keep what the drawing shows as one undo step; Cancel or Esc put the drawing back exactly as it was. The settings sit in a panel at the right; under it Reset puts every setting back to its default, and the two arrows undo and redo the changes made in the dialog box.  The change to the whole selection is one undo step. With a bitmap selected, Ctrl+B opens Brightness/Contrast/Intensity, Ctrl+Shift+B Color Balance and Ctrl+Shift+U Hue/Saturation/Lightness. x: Adding and editing text Adding text Choose the Text tool (F8). For artistic text, click where the text starts and type. Press Enter to start a new line. For paragraph text, drag a frame, then type. The text wraps at the edges of the frame. Press Esc to finish. An empty text is removed. New artistic text is 24 points, paragraph text 12 points, in the first sans-serif font found. Change the defaults by formatting with nothing selected. To make an existing object a text frame, right-click it and choose to create an empty text frame; see Empty frames. Text > Insert Placeholder Text fills the selected frames with sample text, as much as fits. Editing text Click text with the Text tool, or double-click it with the Pick tool, to edit it in place. Text > Edit Text (Ctrl+Shift+T) opens a box with the whole text to edit instead; OK puts it back in the drawing, and the characters you did not change keep their formatting. Typing, Ctrl+V insert at the caret, replacing the selection Ctrl+C, Ctrl+X, Ctrl+V copy, cut and paste the selected characters; the Edit menu, the toolbar and the right-click menu do the same while you edit. Pasted here, they keep their font, size and colors; other programs get their plain text Backspace, Delete delete the selection, else the character before or after Enter, Shift+Enter new paragraph, new line Arrow keys, with Ctrl move by a character or a word; Shift selects Home, End, with Ctrl start or end of the line, or of the text Ctrl+A select all Ctrl+B, Ctrl+I, Ctrl+U bold, italic, underline Ctrl+L, Ctrl+E, Ctrl+R align left, center, right Ctrl+J, Ctrl+H, Ctrl+N full justify, force justify, no alignment Shift+F3 change case (see Writing tools) Double-click select a word A new alignment keeps artistic text in place at the reference point of the X and Y fields of the property bar; in a frame it applies to the paragraphs at the caret. Text in right-to-left scripts (Arabic, Hebrew) is laid out right to left, also when it is mixed with left-to-right words, and selections shade every selected letter. Keyboards and input methods that send characters (such as those for Tamil and other Indian scripts on Windows) type into text and fields, and Alt codes typed on the keypad give their character once. Letters typed with AltGr (Polish ą ę ł, German @ € { }) type into text and fields, also on Windows. On Android the on-screen keyboard types every script its input methods compose (Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Tamil). Older fonts that set the letters of a script at the places of Latin ones (some Tamil fonts) type as their keyboards expect: Autocorrect does not change the letters typed in them. All your typing in one editing session is one undo step. Formatting from the property bar With the Text tool, or with text selected, the property bar has the font list, the size (type it or pick from the list), bold, italic, underline, the alignment (left, center, right, full justify), bullets and drop cap for paragraph text, Text (Ctrl+T) and Edit Text. The button beside the font size opens the sliders of a variable font's axes (see Variable fonts). While editing, they act on the selected characters; otherwise on the whole selected texts, and only the setting you change: a new font for several texts keeps each one's size, bold and italic. Your choice also becomes the default for the next text. The font list shows each family in its own font, with the ones you used last at the top. Type to narrow the list. A family with several styles has an arrow that shows them. See Fonts and glyphs. The Text panel The Text panel (Ctrl+T) has every text setting, in three sections you can open and close: Character, Paragraph and Frame. The three buttons at the top show the panel from that section on. Full justification spreads Chinese and Japanese lines to the edge of the frame by adding room between the characters, and paragraph text in those scripts breaks lines by their rules: punctuation such as ，。、 and closing brackets never start a line, and opening brackets never end one. Letters given another color keep the font's kerning with their neighbours.  Character: the font, style and size; range kerning (-50 to 200%) and underline; the fill, background and outline of the characters. More options under the section: character offsets and angle, strikethrough and OpenType features. Paragraph: the alignment (none, left, center, right, full justify, and forced justify, which spreads the last line too); line spacing in percent of the character height, points or percent of the font size; left, first-line and right indents; space before and after paragraphs; character and word spacing. The gear opens custom hyphens. Frame, for paragraph text: the background color of the frame, the vertical alignment (top, middle, bottom), fit text to frame, columns (1 to 8) and the gap between them, and links to the bullets, drop cap and columns dialog boxes, and hyphenation. Every change applies to the selected characters while editing, or to the selected texts, and is one undo step. With no text selected, the settings become those of new text. The button at the top right gives new text the settings of the selected text. Paragraph text frames Frames show as dashed lines. A frame turns red, with a small tab under its bottom edge, when its text does not fit; the text that does not fit is not drawn, printed or exported. To make it fit: drag the frame's handles to enlarge it. The text flows again; the letters keep their size; choose Text > Paragraph Text Frame > Fit Text to Frame to resize the text to fill the frame; link the frame to another one, so the text flows on: Link. Unlink breaks the link. Or click the small tab under the frame's bottom edge, then click another frame (on this page or another one) or click or drag on an empty spot for a new frame: the text flows on into it. You can also drag from the tab and let go over another frame or an empty spot. a picked frame also has a small tab over its top edge: click it, then click the frame

x: Tabs, columns, bullets and drop caps The Text menu has four dialog boxes for laying out paragraph text. Each acts on the selected paragraph text. Their settings are also in the Frame section of the Text panel. Tabs Text > Tabs sets where the Tab character jumps to. At first there is a tab stop every 12.7 mm (half an inch). Select the paragraph text. Choose Text > Tabs. Under Tab stops, change the positions, or click Add tab to add one. Click Close.  Columns Text > Columns splits a text frame into columns; the text flows from one column into the next. Select the paragraph text. Choose Text > Columns. Set the number of Columns and the Gutter, the space between columns (5 mm at first). Click Close.  To break to the next column at a given place, insert Column/Frame Break from Insert Formatting Code. Bullets Text > Bullets puts a bullet before each paragraph. Select the paragraph text. Choose Text > Bullets. Tick Use bullets, and set the bullet Symbol and the Indent (5 mm at first). Click Close.  Drop caps A drop cap is a large first letter that spans several lines. Select the paragraph text. Choose Text > Drop Cap. Tick Use drop cap and set the Lines dropped (3 at first). Click Close. The letter is scaled so its top meets the top of the first line and it sits on the baseline of the last line it spans; the lines beside it are shortened to make room.  Hyphenation Text > Use Hyphenation lets the selected text's words break at the end of lines (while you type in a text, the paragraphs at the cursor; with no text selected, it is the setting for new text), with at least two letters before and three after the break. A comma or other punctuation next to a word does not stop it from breaking, and words with an apostrophe (such as Italian dell'anno) break too. Words with a capital letter are never broken. To decide yourself where a word may break, see Custom hyphens.

h: The Fonts panel Font lists and the filter Variable fonts Missing fonts The Font Sampler The Glyphs panel The Font Manager
x: Fonts and glyphs TraceDraw uses the fonts installed on your computer, fonts you add in the Font Manager, and fonts that come with a drawing. This page explains the panels and the dialog box for working with fonts and special characters. The Fonts panel The Fonts panel lists the font families.  Type in the filter field to narrow the list. Under Fonts in document are the families the drawing uses. A family that is not installed is marked missing; its text shows in a similar font and keeps its font name. A family that came with the drawing is marked embedded. Click a family to give it to the selected text, or to make it the font of new text. Font lists and the filter The font lists of the property bar, the Text panel, the Glyphs panel and the options work the same way: Type to jump to a family. The last five families you picked are at the top ("used last"), and every family's name is drawn in its own font. The mouse wheel over the closed list picks the next or previous family for the text being edited or selected. A font that came with the drawing and is not installed says "Embedded" at the end of its row and after its name in the font box: its text is drawn with the copy that came with the drawing. The Filter button at the top of the open list shows the filter's choices beside the list. Each click filters at once and leaves the list open; the button counts the choices made, such as "Filter (2)", and Clear filter at the top of the choices removes them. The choices, in sections that fold: Fonts shown: all fonts, installed fonts, the fonts in this drawing, or in the browser version the fonts to download. Style: serif, sans serif, script, decorative, monospaced, symbol. Weight: light, regular, bold. Width: condensed, normal, expanded. Technology: TrueType, OpenType, variable. Scripts: Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Hebrew, Arabic, Devanagari, Bengali, Thai, Korean, Japanese, Chinese and symbols. OpenType features: ligatures, kerning, small capitals, the kinds of figures, fractions, superscripts and subscripts, ordinals, slashed zero, swashes, alternates and stylistic sets, each on its own. Embedding rights: installable, editable, preview and print, restricted, bitmap only. Folders: the folders the fonts are in, as the Font Manager lists them: each folder you added to the libraries and the system's font folders, not their subfolders. Within a section a family needs one of the ticked choices (every ticked one for the OpenType features), and it needs what every section asks. The values are read from the font files themselves; with thousands of fonts the list fills in over a moment the first time. Variable fonts A variable font holds a range of weights, widths and other designs in one file. To set them on text: Select the text, or the letters, in a variable font. Click the button beside the font size on the property bar (or in the first section of the Text panel). It is greyed out, with a tip saying why, when the font is not variable. The Character section of the Text panel shows the same sliders. Drag the slider of an axis: Weight, Width, Slant, Italic, Optical size, or the font's own axes by the names it gives them, each over the font's range. The text follows the slider while you drag, so you can judge it on the page. Letting go of the slider, or typing a value, keeps it as one undo step. Default axes takes the values off. The values are saved in .tdraw files and drawn in exports and PDF files; a weight set this way replaces the bold TraceDraw would otherwise draw. Missing fonts When a drawing uses fonts that are not installed, the Missing Fonts dialog box asks which installed font draws each one, for this session or for good. See Missing fonts. Install the fonts and the text shows in them again. Drawings saved as .tdraw, and .cdr files with embedded fonts, can carry their fonts along. The Font Sampler The Font Sampler panel (Text > Font Sampler) shows a line of sample text in several fonts, one under the other, to compare them.  Type the sample text at the top; left empty, a sentence in your interface language is used. Set the size (10 to 96, 28 at first). Add fonts by typing part of a name and clicking one of the matches (up to 24 fonts); the cross removes one. At first the panel lists the text font and the fonts of the drawing. Click a sample to give that font to the selected text. The Glyphs panel The Glyphs panel (Text > Glyphs, Ctrl+F11) shows every character of a font, to insert symbols and special characters.  Choose the font. Choose a character range: the entire font, Basic Latin, Latin-1 Supplement, Latin Extended, Greek, Cyrillic, Hebrew, Arabic, punctuation, numbers, currency, arrows, mathematical operators or symbols. Click a character. It is inserted at the caret of the text you are editing, or as a new text in the middle of the page. Hover a character to see its name and code. A small arrow under a character means the font has alternates for it (such as swashes or small capitals); click it to see them. The glyphs you used last are at the top of the panel. Under the grid, drag the slider to make the characters larger or smaller, and click Copy to put the character you clicked last on the clipboard, to paste it in another program. Type in the search field above the grid to find characters: type the characters themselves (such as é), or a Unicode code point such as U+20AC, 0x20ac or 20AC. The line above the grid shows the code point, the character and the range of the character under the pointer. The Font Manager Tools > Font Manager opens the Font Manager, a window that organizes your fonts.  Libraries (top left): My fonts (the installed fonts), the folders you added, Favorites and your collections. Double-click a collection to rename it; right-click for more. Filters (bottom left): by status (installed, not installed, protected system fonts, duplicates), embedding rights, technology (TrueType, OpenType, variable), weight, width, style, character range and OpenType features. h: Choosing the fonts that stand in Turning the dialog box off and on Other ways to deal with missing fonts
x: Missing fonts A drawing made on another computer can use fonts that are not installed on yours. TraceDraw always shows such text in an installed font that looks close, and keeps the text's own font name. When the drawing opens, the Missing Fonts dialog box lets you choose which installed font draws each missing one, for now or for good. Choosing the fonts that stand in When you open a drawing with missing fonts, the Missing Fonts dialog box lists them: Each row shows the Missing font and the font it is Drawn with now. The first choice in the list is the font TraceDraw picked by itself, marked "(automatic)": a font drawn to the same widths when there is one, else one of the same style. To use another font, open the list of the row and click an installed family. Type part of a name in Find a font to narrow the lists. Choose how long the choice holds: For this session only (the drawing keeps its fonts) (the default): the font you chose draws the text until TraceDraw closes, bold and italic text included. The drawing keeps its own font names, so it is saved with them and shows in its own fonts on a computer that has them. Replace in the drawing (saved with it): every text in the missing family, also in groups, clip frames, tables and symbols, takes the font you chose. This changes the drawing and undoes in one step. Click OK. Cancel, Esc or the close button change nothing: the automatic fonts stay. Either way, the status bar then names the fonts still missing and the fonts that draw them, or says they were replaced. When some objects of the file could not be read, their note follows the dialog box. Turning the dialog box off and on Tick Do not show this message again in the dialog box to stop it. The drawing then opens straight away and the status bar names the missing fonts. Click that note on the status bar to open the Warnings page of Tools > Options > Global, where Ask which installed font draws each missing one (the Missing Fonts dialog) turns the dialog box on again (it is on at first). When an opened drawing uses fonts that are not installed, on the same page, is a separate, plain message that only names the missing fonts after the drawing opens. Opening drawings from scripts, the command line or the AI connection never stops at this dialog box. Other ways to deal with missing fonts Install the fonts, or add their folder in the Font Manager (see Fonts and glyphs); the text then shows in them. In the Fonts panel, families the drawing uses that are not installed are marked missing. Drawings saved as .tdraw and .cdr files with Embed fonts carry their fonts along, and a package holds the font files in its Fonts folder. The preflight lists text in fonts that are not installed before you print or publish.

x: Writing tools TraceDraw checks spelling and grammar, finds synonyms, corrects as you type, and fixes text that came in with the wrong characters. The commands are in Text > Writing Tools and the Text menu. The Writing Tools dialog box Text > Writing Tools > Spell Check, Grammar and Thesaurus open the Writing Tools dialog box at that tab. Check chooses whether to check every text of the page (Document) or only the selected texts (Selection).  Spell Checker Click Start. The first word not found shows, with suggestions under Replacements. Click a suggestion to put it in Replace with (double-click to replace at once), or type the right word. Click Replace for this place, Auto Replace for every place, Skip Once or Skip All to leave it, or Add to add the word to your own word list. Undo takes back the last replacement. Options has Ignore words with numbers, Ignore words in capitals and Add corrections to Autocorrect. Dictionaries TraceDraw checks spelling with Hunspell dictionaries: for each language a .dic file and an .aff file with the same name, such as pt_BR.dic and pt_BR.aff. Free dictionaries for most languages can be downloaded from the projects that make them; other programs often install them too. Open Tools > Options > Text > Spelling. Click Open Folder and copy the .dic and .aff files into that folder (folders inside it work too), or name a folder that already has dictionaries in Also read dictionaries from. Click Read Again. The Dictionaries list shows each one; clear a box to stop using it. A word is right when any dictionary in use knows it. Dictionaries installed on your system are used as well. Without any, only a built-in word list is used. Hyphenation dictionaries (hyph_ files such as hyph_pt_BR.dic) go in the same folders. Choose one under Text > Paragraph Text > Hyphenation patterns to hyphenate text in that language. Grammar The grammar checker finds doubled words, double spaces, spaces before punctuation, missing spaces after it, sentences that start in lower case, unbalanced brackets and quotes, repeated punctuation, sentences over 40 words, missing end marks and, in English, "a" and "an" before the wrong sound. For each finding it shows the replacement, the New sentence and the Rule Name. Click Start (then Replace), Skip Once or Skip Rule. Thesaurus Type a word (the first word of the selected text at first) and click Look Up. The meanings show with their synonyms: click one to pick it, double-click to look it up. Insert puts it in the text, keeping the capitals. Under Options, Close after inserting closes the dialog box after inserting, and Choose Thesaurus File uses a thesaurus file you have. Autocorrect Text > Writing Tools > Autocorrect opens the Autocorrect tab of Tools > Options > Text, which sets what is corrected while you type: Capitalize first letter of sentences; Correct two initial capitals ("THe" becomes "The"); Capitalize names of days ("monday" becomes "Monday"); Automatically create hyperlinks when typing web addresses: typing www.example.com or an address starting with http:// or https:// gives the text object that hyperlink, unless it has one; Language the language whose quotation marks are used (the interface language unless you pick another); Use typographic quotation marks, and Use straight quotation marks after numbers (e.g. 6'); Single quotes and Double quotes: the Open and Close marks, if you want others than the language's; the Replacement table, used when Replace text while typing is on: (c) becomes ©, (r) ®, (tm) ™, 1/2 ½ and so on. Type in Replace and With, then click Add; click a row to Delete it, or change its text and click Replace. Apply to Selection applies the rules to the selected text. Text you paste or import is never changed.  Custom hyphens Text > Custom Optional Hyphens (also the gear of the Paragraph section of the Text panel) defines where your own words may break, such as product names. Those words break only there when hyphenation is on. Choose the Language (Show all languages lists every one). Type the Word and the Hyphenated Word with hyphens where it may break, such as Trace-Draw. Click Add Definition. Remove Definition removes the selected definition. Under Automatically insert custom optional hyphens, When typing and When pasting and importing text turn hyphenation on for texts that hold a defined word. Click Apply to Selection to apply them to the selected text now, or OK to keep them.  Change case Text > Change Case (Shift+F3) changes the selected text to Sentence case, lowercase, UPPERCASE, Title Case or tOGGLE cASE.  Text statistics Text > Text Statistics counts the text objects, lines, words, characters and fonts of the selected text, or of the page.  Encode Text that came from another program sometimes shows the wrong characters, such as "cafÃ©" instead of "café". Text > Encode fixes it: Select the text. Choose how the text Text was read as and what It really is (UTF-8, Windows-1252, ISO-8859-1, Mac OS Roman or Windows-1251). Check the Preview and click OK.  Web-compatible text Text > Make Text Web-compatible simplifies the selected text for web pages: gradient, pattern, texture and mesh fills become a flat color, and outlines, shadows and effects are removed.

Sjablonen en stijlen Sjablonen en stijlen besparen werk dat u anders zou herhalen. Een sjabloon is een kant-en-klare tekening om mee te beginnen. Een stijl is een benoemde set van vulling, omtrek en transparantie die gekoppeld blijft aan de objecten die hem gebruiken, zodat één wijziging ze allemaal aanpast. De standaardeigenschappen bepalen hoe nieuwe objecten eruitzien. Kleurstijlen, die voor losse kleuren op dezelfde manier werken, worden uitgelegd in Kleurstijlen.

x: Templates A template is a drawing to start from: a blank page of a common size, or a designed business card, flyer, poster, letterhead or label to fill in. Opening a template makes a new, untitled drawing; the template itself never changes. Starting from a template Choose File > New from Template, or click New from Template on the Welcome Screen. Find a template: type in Search templates to match names and categories; choose where templates come from: All templates, Built in or My templates; choose a category, or All categories. Click a template to see it. With Show template details on, the pane on the right shows it large with its Category, Page size and Source. Click Open, double-click the template, or press Enter. The Size slider at the bottom makes the thumbnails larger or smaller, and Open template opens any .tdt or .tdraw file as a template.  The built-in templates Blank pages: A4 portrait and landscape, A3, Letter, business card (90 by 50 mm), A2 poster, web (1920 by 1080 pixels) and social media (1080 by 1080 pixels). Designed: two business cards, a sale flyer and an event flyer, a poster, a letterhead, a certificate, an invoice, a birthday banner, a quote post and a round label. They are made of ordinary shapes and text with sample text, so you can change every part. Saving your own templates Make the drawing you want to start from in the future. Choose File > Save as Template. Give it a name and save it. Templates you save appear under My templates. They are kept in the templates folder of your settings, so they are not available in the browser version.

x: Object styles and default properties The Object Styles panel has two parts: the Default Properties of new objects, and the styles of the drawing. Both are saved with the drawing. Open it from Window > Panels, or right-click an object and choose the object styles panel.  Default properties New objects take the fill and outline of their kind: Graphic: shapes, lines, tables and everything except text no fill, a thin black outline Artistic text: text without a frame black fill, no outline Paragraph text: text in a frame black fill, no outline In the panel, each kind shows its fill and outline, with From Selection (take the fill and outline of the selected object) and Reset (back to the defaults of a new drawing). Changing defaults with nothing selected When nothing is selected and you choose a fill or outline (click a palette color, use a fill tool, change the outline color or width), the change goes to new objects. TraceDraw asks which kinds of new objects it applies to: Tick Graphic, Artistic text and Paragraph text as needed. The kinds you ticked last time are ticked. Tick Use these kinds from now on without asking to skip the question from now on. Click OK. Cancel changes nothing.  The check box Ask which kinds a change with nothing selected applies to in the panel turns the question on or off. The Properties panel with nothing selected also edits the Graphic defaults. To keep the defaults for every new drawing, choose Tools > Save Settings as Default. Styles A style is a named set of properties: Fill, Outline (its color, width, line style and arrowheads) and Transparency. Objects you give a style stay linked to it: change the style and they all change. To make a style Select an object with the look you want. Click New style from selection. The style is named "Style 1" and so on, takes the fill, outline and transparency of the object, and is linked to every selected object. Using and changing styles Each style shows its swatches, its name (click it to rename), how many objects are linked to it, and its parts as check boxes: Apply gives the selection the style and links it. Update from selection takes the fill, outline and transparency of the selected object; every linked object follows. Turning a part off leaves that property to each object. Delete removes the style; linked objects keep their look. Break Link to Style unlinks the selected objects, which keep their look. You can still change a linked object directly; the next change of its style sets the style's parts again. Right-click an object to apply a style from its menu.

Pagina's en lay-out Een tekening kan veel pagina's hebben, elk met een eigen formaat en stand. Deze pagina's leggen uit hoe u pagina's toevoegt, ordent en nummert, de documentopties instelt (paginaformaat, lay-out, achtergrond, afloop, linialen, raster en hulplijnen), hulplijnen plaatst, objecten laat uitlijnen en de eigenschappen van een tekening leest.
